records.reason: Measure m204 at 1/1 with 50.05 mg. Together with the matched 100.1 mg row, this tests the strong alcohol loading effect suggested by the measured m204 row 73502a52708e4f9c2391 and the m120 loading pair 71abc36775b6cce56da7/e4fd83fb3852eb354a66.

Measure the same m204 condition at 100.1 mg. The predictor gives nearly the same endpoints as the lower-load row, so this controlled pair can teach whether loading dependence transfers from the observed alcohol examples.

Measure m120 at 1/1 and 166.95 mg to extend the observed m120 5/1 loading contrast. It tests whether the large endpoint change between 71abc36775b6cce56da7 and e4fd83fb3852eb354a66 also depends on solvent ratio.

Measure m160 at 5/1 under the same 100 mg loading as the measured 2/1 row 2feb7d8e0a3566ddf97f. This supplies a condition-response point for an amino benzonitrile where the model currently predicts a large shift.
Measure m86 at 2/1 with 117 mg, complementing the measured 5/1 amino ester at 9bc73e0c27d4d6b44abb. The pair tests whether the large underprediction is retained across solvent strength.

Measure m141 at 10/1 and low loading after the measured 5/1 m141 label 65f4f125b5e1f8137bd9. This probes the solvent response of a basic heteroaromatic scaffold that is likely to be position and condition dependent.
Measure an unobserved fused pyridyl-biphenyl scaffold at 5/1. It adds connected coverage of basic aromatic environments beyond the quinoline failures 04a2e8ad27ca641a3a12 and 1ae3618ec277b0463686.
Measure m88 at 2/1 using the same nominal loading as the measured 1/1 amino ester 9a9324fbb6b1e17e7743. This gives a clean local condition contrast within the amino ester family.
Measure m89 at 2/1 with the same 111.7 mg loading as the measured 5/1 row 3aed7873d2fd1cf48684. The result tests whether amino ester retention changes smoothly with solvent strength.

Measure m177 at 0/1 with the same 140.6 mg loading and DCM volume used in the measured 10/1 row ce14dd2481560a984aea. This directly extends the nitrobenzophenone endpoint curve after the large V2 failures in ce14dd2481560a984aea and aa43fe84c0d8c825fe58.

Measure the multifunctional ester and ketone m13 at 10/1. Its broad predicted endpoint range targets undercovered high-HBA chemistry and tests whether the model's broad V2 behavior transfers beyond the observed carbonyl failures.

Measure m125 at 5/1 and 150 mg. It fills a condition gap between the observed m125 rows f4fb5c03b8e8996e75f6, e7ed7ca4a53258b73ba2, and 69b09343d0b9995c3ae4, where V2 changes sharply and are poorly predicted.

Measure m173 at 10/1 with the same 124.75 mg loading used by the measured cinnamic acid condition series. It tests whether the large V2 response seen across f90a5a5a54509c085ebd, 1e775e7d8dcbf48fd6f8, and 0b247863fd6e8aaf44d8 continues at a stronger PE-rich condition.

Measure acetoxybenzaldehyde at 5/1 after the measured 10/1 row 351c17dfa8f46a8cb40a, whose V1 and V2 were both substantially underpredicted. This tests whether the combined aldehyde/ester interaction has a transferable solvent response.

Measure diphenyl sulfoxide at 2/1 with 50 mg, extending the measured 5/1 sulfoxide outlier f82cfd3b57735b0ead3c. The matched scaffold condition curve can separate a persistent S=O interaction error from a single-condition anomaly.

Measure diphenyl sulfoxide at 0/1 with the same loading as f82cfd3b57735b0ead3c and the other selected sulfoxide row. Two weaker-solvent points will constrain the condition response of this underrepresented functional group.

Measure chalcone at 20/1 to extend the observed 1/1 and 10/1 labels 067c9b96b35fefd28fdf and 0dfdfd6dce2d3f41a427. The high-onset transfer hypothesis was rejected, but the finish response remains unresolved.

Measure dibenzalacetone at 20/1 after the observed 1/1 and 10/1 rows 3f6b817d855e67b3b406 and 7726f4a207a737256a86. This tests the remaining V2 response while avoiding further reliance on the rejected high-V1 analogy.

Measure m67 at 20/1 to extend the observed accessible alcohol label 5e784130c58b8175024e. It tests whether the model's predicted later finish transfers across a stronger-solvent condition for a secondary alcohol.
Measure the amino acrylate m72 at 10/1 with a 51.1 mg loading. Its wide predicted V1 and V2 ranges add coverage for a donor-containing unsaturated ester with no direct high-strength-condition label.

Measure the phenolic trifluoromethyl ether m209 at 50/1 and high loading. This adds a phenol/ether environment with broad predicted endpoints and tests transfer among donor-containing aromatic acceptors.

Measure nitrobenzyl alcohol m200 at 1/1. The combination of a nitro group and accessible alcohol is chemically distinct from the observed alcohol failures and can test joint donor/acceptor representation.

Measure cyano benzophenone m159 at 50/1. It extends the observed m159 condition coverage into a weak-solvent regime and probes whether a nitrile plus benzophenone is represented as an unusually retained polyacceptor.
Measure the methoxybenzophenone m114 at 50/1. Its large predicted V1 and V2 with wide endpoint ranges target sparse polyaromatic carbonyl coverage relevant to overall model transfer.

Measure the multifunctional benzophenone m178 at 50/1. This adds a high-loading, weak-solvent polycarbonyl point and tests whether broad predicted finishes are supported outside the known nitro and aldehyde examples.
Measure the fused ether aldehyde m194 at 5/1. It is chemically distinct and low-similarity, providing a focused transfer test for simultaneous aldehyde and cyclic ether interactions.

Measure the phosphorus-containing aromatic m202 at 10/1. Its low structural similarity and acceptor-rich functionality expand representation coverage without duplicating the dominant carbonyl families.
Measure brominated methylenedioxybenzene m6 at 10/1. This tests constrained ether geometry and halogen substitution against the simpler anisole and fused-ether observations.

Measure ethyl cinnamate m73 at 10/1 and low loading between the measured 1/1 and 50/1 labels 2cf789c87f7c6325c020 and e6dcf9d6f65fa598a38e. It helps distinguish a molecule-specific cinnamate anomaly from a general conjugated ester response.

Measure cyanoacetophenone m31 at 5/1 after the measured 1/1 row 434c05a62ac9e65dd102. This supplies condition coverage for an aromatic ketone bearing an exposed nitrile and can improve acceptor accessibility transfer.
Measure amino ester m104 at 20/1 and 175.2 mg. It extends the amino ester/basic interaction regime beyond the observed m104 labels and tests whether the model underestimates V2 at weaker solvent.
Measure cyclic ether carbonyl m181 at 10/1 with half the loading volume of the measured 10/1 row 989b2145455d703d3b6d. This is a controlled loading contrast for a cyclic acceptor environment.

hypotheses.content: Elution finish, especially V2, is strongly scaffold and condition dependent; the current model can miss broad intervals and abrupt endpoint changes even when V1 is moderately close.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: V2 errors dominate several large observed residuals, so condition-response labels around these scaffolds can teach endpoint-specific corrections that generalize across the row distribution.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the selected m173, m177, m125, and m28 condition points reveal transferable V2 trends or separate scaffold-specific response functions?

hypotheses.content: The unusually high 1/1 onset predicted for chalcone and dibenzalacetone was transferred from an ethyl cinnamate pattern and does not generalize to conjugated ketones; their remaining V2 solvent response is unresolved.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Removing this false structural transfer can improve V1 generalization, while additional V2 labels can preserve useful solvent-response information from the same family.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: After the onset analogy is removed, do chalcone and dibenzalacetone still share a predictable V2 response at weaker solvent?

hypotheses.content: Loading amount can change both endpoints substantially in a scaffold-dependent way; the effect is not a universal constant correction.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The m120 pair shows a large endpoint change at fixed recorded mobile phase and loading solvent, so controlled loading pairs can improve use of the density-times-volume feature.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the m204 and m181 loading contrasts reproduce a large endpoint shift in other alcohol and cyclic-acceptor environments?

hypotheses.content: Steric shielding of mesityl ketone does not support the predicted earlier onset in weaker mobile phase; the observed condition response instead moves onset and finish later together.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: This rejects an unsupported local structural correction and reduces the risk of encoding an inverse solvent response for crowded aromatic ketones.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do other substituted aryl ketones follow the observed monotonic endpoint shift rather than the rejected steric-shielding pattern?

hypotheses.content: Basic and amino-containing scaffolds require environment-specific response modeling. Quinoline and amino ester rows are strongly underpredicted, while the matched aminobenzonitriles do not show an equally large positional effect.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: These labels can teach the graph model to distinguish basic-ring topology, nitrogen accessibility, and substitution environment instead of applying a nitrogen-count correction.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the selected quinoline-like, amino ester, and aminobenzonitrile condition points separate scaffold topology effects from solvent-response effects?

hypotheses.content: Alcohol retention depends on OH structural environment and loading context; accessible primary, secondary benzylic, and ether-substituted alcohols can behave very differently.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Alcohol rows occupy a broad retention range and expose failures in both donor-environment transfer and loading response, affecting many catalog rows.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do m204, m120, m67, and m209 labels establish a transferable distinction between free OH accessibility and neighboring ether or aromatic groups?

hypotheses.content: Diphenyl sulfoxide has a silica-interaction response that is poorly represented by the current descriptors and does not transfer reliably from carbonyl or ether analogues.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: A condition curve on the same sulfoxide can identify whether the large observed error is a functional-group representation failure or a local solvent-response failure.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the selected 0/1 and 2/1 sulfoxide rows remain much later than predicted, or does the large residual collapse outside 5/1?

feedback_interpretation: The new labels changed the plan substantially. The predicted high V1 transfer from ethyl cinnamate to chalcone and dibenzalacetone was contradicted: both ketones started near 5 to 6 mL, so H2 is rejected for onset, although their V2 response remains worth mapping. The mesityl ketone pair also contradicted the proposed steric-shielding onset decrease, rejecting H4. In contrast, the m120 pair showed a large controlled loading effect, supporting conditional use of loading amount. Quinoline and amino ester rows were strongly underpredicted, supporting scaffold-specific basic-nitrogen modeling, while aminobenzonitrile labels were much less discrepant. Large V2 errors in cinnamic acid, nitrobenzophenone, dimethoxybenzaldehyde, acetoxybenzaldehyde, and the sulfoxide shifted the batch toward V2-focused condition curves and functional-group repairs.
batch_rationale: The batch combines failure repair with scientifically connected local experiments. Controlled loading contrasts for m204, m120, and m181 test whether the observed loading effect transfers across alcohol and cyclic-acceptor environments. Condition curves for m173, m177, m125, m28, and m199 target the catalog regions where measured V2 errors were largest, while the chalcone and dibenzalacetone follow-ups separate the rejected onset analogy from any remaining finish response. Basic nitrogen rows cover quinoline-like, amino ester, and aminobenzonitrile environments. The remaining choices add low-similarity sulfoxide, phosphorus, nitro-alcohol, fused ether, polycarbonyl, and halogenated ether chemistry. This mix should improve structure-condition-loading transfer and endpoint-specific calibration across the Row-distribution rather than concentrating labels on one predicted outcome.
